decisions.evidence: It states, “A fixed finite basis can be changed with only constant-factor size and depth overhead.” This is false for arbitrary finite bases: {AND,0,1} cannot express NOT, whereas the stated basis can. Mutual constant-overhead simulation requires a qualification such as functionally complete, mutually simulable bases. Confirmed against the cited dependency and repaired in the live carrier: The definition now limits constant-overhead basis changes to fixed bounded-arity bases that mutually simulate one another, with the functionally complete case stated as an example.

It defines a transcript as “the previous messages together with the verifier randomness already used” and then defines a prover strategy as a function on “every transcript at a prover turn.” For a private-coin verifier this lets the purported prover read hidden coins. In the isomorphic-graph no-case, a full transcript contains the hidden challenge bit b and permutation pi, so this function can return b and win with probability 1; an actual prover sees only H and succeeds with probability at most 1/2. Thus this is not the prover-strategy model for private-coin interactive proofs. Confirmed against the cited dependency and repaired in the live carrier: The definition now makes the transcript a public view only: exchanged messages and revealed coins are included, hidden verifier coins and private work states are excluded, and a prover strategy is a function of that public view.

The definition says nodes are labelled by transcripts and that “The root value is the protocol's maximum acceptance probability.” Its dependency defines those transcripts to include verifier randomness already used. Hence the tree maximizes separately at nodes differing only in hidden verifier coins. For the private-coin graph-nonisomorphism protocol on isomorphic graphs, that tree has value 1 by choosing the hidden b at each prover node, while every actual prover has acceptance probability at most 1/2. The asserted identification of root value with protocol maximum acceptance probability is false. Confirmed against the cited dependency and repaired in the live carrier: The game is now defined on public information states with conditional distributions over compatible hidden verifier histories; each prover maximum chooses one response per public view, so its root value is the legal protocol value.

Step 2.1 says, “Accept precisely when that value exceeds 1/2.” But the value supplied by the cited game-tree definition is a full-information value because its prover nodes are labelled by transcripts containing hidden verifier randomness. On two independent graph-nonisomorphism challenges for an isomorphic graph pair, the actual protocol has soundness at most 1/4, whereas this game tree has root value 1 by answering each hidden challenge bit. The proposed PSPACE test can therefore accept a no-instance; the inference from the computed tree value to IP soundness is not licensed. Confirmed against the cited dependency and repaired in the live carrier: The proof now computes the public-information game value, explicitly averaging compatible private histories while maximizing only over public-view responses, and the 1/2 test is licensed by the IP gap.
